title: Defining Everest: A Reflection on the Challenges of Teaching
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart uses Hillary and Norgay's 1953 ascent to argue that, in one respect, the earnest teacher faces a harder task: the climbers had one clear goal, while a teacher aims at thousands of shifting ones. He lists them - state test targets that moved from ACT to SAT mid-year, a succession of 'Common-Core-aligned' assessments, and separate district, building, and department goals. Under all of these sit the students' own futures, the vocations many have not yet discovered. He calls that long-term flourishing the real point of school, while admitting it resists measurement, and illustrates it with a coach who says to ask him in twenty years how his team turned out. He does not dismiss data as the enemy, but argues that teachers who fail to define their own Everest in a single sentence are the ones most likely to burn out. His practical answer is to be explicit and selective about the most critical literacy, thinking, and character skills and the core content knowledge for each course.
points: The Everest comparison makes a point about clarity rather than difficulty: a four-year-old can understand the climbers' goal, but a teacher struggles to state a year's aim with the same precision.

Stuart gives a concrete case of shifting targets - his state switched from the ACT to the SAT mid-year after cycling through Smarter Balanced and MSTEP - to show how external goals move under teachers' feet.
He links burnout directly to losing one's own definition of the work, reporting that his worst stretches of the year came when he lost sight of his Everest.
Data keeps a legitimate place in his account as a science teachers should practice and debate, but he argues it cannot define the job's ultimate aim.

His remedy is disciplined selectivity: name the few most critical literacy, thinking, and character skills and power standards per course, which makes the job more doable and students' K-12 experience more coherent.
quotes: Though the execution of it was unprecedented, Hillary and Norgay's goal was beautifully simple: they intended to set foot atop the Earth's highest place. I can explain their accomplishment to my four-year-old, and she can comprehend it with accuracy.

Yet when I attempt to explain to my four-year-old, with similar accuracy and clarity, what it is that I tried to accomplish as a teacher this past school year, I'm hard-pressed. This past year, I didn't aim at a single Everest — I aimed at thousands.
However, midway through the year, my state announced a switch to the SAT. The tectonic plates shifted; Everest moved.
This is what I mean by long-term flourishing. This is the actual point of schools, though it's hard to collect data on.

That sounds about right. Ask me in twenty years if I was successful during the 2014-2015 school year, if I did my job, which is to be one more encouraging, empowering adult in a child's schooling, to be one more teacher who shows them how to think, read, write, speak, and develop character.

But Everest for us is way more than data points and school categorizations, and if we as educators don't define Everest for ourselves — if we don't, in a single sentence, reduce our work into its essence — I think we're way more likely to lose ourselves in this job. The times when I became most burnt out this past year were the times when I most lost sight of my own definition of Everest.

We need to define Everest; we need to be specific and picky about what our students will become excellent at this year in math or art or physical education. It may never be as clear as it was for Hillary and Norgay, but I know we can do better than we are right now.
